script.opening: “I need a steroid injection in this shoulder. My client had one and it was like magic. I can’t lift my arm to blow-dry and I’m losing clients. And before you ask, I don’t want any blood tests.”

facts.text: Left shoulder. Started as an ache four months ago, then increasingly painful, worse at night, can’t lie on it. Over the last six weeks it has become stiff: cannot reach behind her back, fasten her bra, or lift her arm above shoulder height. No fall or injury. Right-handed.
No weight loss she has noticed, no cough, no fever, no hot red joint, no arm weakness or numbness, no chest pain or breathlessness on exertion, no history of cancer. Neck is fine.
Owns a two-chair salon; one junior. Cut her hours by half. Lost three regular clients. Rent and a loan for the salon. “If I stop, I lose the business.”
Ibuprofen and paracetamol on and off, helps a bit. Hot water bottle. Has not seen a physiotherapist. Was going to pay for an MRI.
Thirsty for months, up twice a night to wee, tired, “but I’m 54 and I work all day”. Overweight. No blurred vision, no foot problems. Smokes 5 a day.
Her mother had type 2 diabetes and had a leg amputated at 68. Lorraine knows the earlier blood test was “borderline” and has ignored the letters: “If I don’t know, I don’t have to deal with it.”

Brisk and businesslike, pushes for the injection. Bristles at blood tests. Softens if the doctor asks what worries her about them and links the test to the shoulder. Agrees to an HbA1c if she understands how it helps and that diabetes found early is very different from her mother’s experience.

ice.ideas: “It’s worn out from 30 years of hairdressing. An injection will fix it.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA: fear of diabetes because of her mother’s amputation, which is why she has avoided blood tests; also losing the business.
ice.expectations: “An injection now, maybe an MRI, and no blood tests.”

cues: “I don’t want any blood tests” before anyone has suggested one — something lies behind it.
Unanswered recall letters and a borderline HbA1c in the record.
Thirst and nocturia mentioned as “just being 54”.
“I’m losing clients” — work and money are central.

checkpoints.text: Takes a focused history and remote examination showing painful global restriction of active movement, particularly external rotation, consistent with frozen shoulder; arranges face-to-face examination to confirm passive restriction if needed
Screens for red flags: trauma, fever or hot joint, weight loss or history of cancer, neurological symptoms, referred pain (neck, cardiac, Pancoast)
Explores the refusal of blood tests and uncovers the fear of diabetes linked to her mother’s amputation; asks about osmotic symptoms
Explains the association between frozen shoulder and diabetes, and that a steroid injection can raise blood glucose for some days, as reasons to check HbA1c now

Discusses options honestly: analgesia, physiotherapy and home exercises, and an intra-articular corticosteroid injection, which can reduce pain in the early painful phase; explains that MRI is not usually needed for a clinical diagnosis
Explains the natural history (painful, stiff and recovery phases over months to a few years) and when referral is considered (persistent severe symptoms despite treatment)
Supports work: practical adjustments, pacing, a fit note with “may be fit for work” and suggested adaptations if useful, and signposting for self-employed support
Respects her autonomy, links the plan to her goal of keeping the business, and safety-nets (red flags, osmotic symptoms worsening, no improvement)

worked.txt: “You said you don’t want blood tests before I’d mentioned any. Can I ask what makes you feel that way?”
“That must have been awful to see with your mum. It makes complete sense that you’d rather not know. Can I tell you how different it is when diabetes is found early?”
“Frozen shoulder is more common in people with diabetes or borderline sugars, and a steroid injection can push sugar up for a few days. So checking your sugar helps me do the injection safely.”
“An injection into the joint can ease the pain in this early stage, which may let you work and do your exercises. It doesn’t cure the stiffness on its own, so physio exercises matter too.”
“The diagnosis is made from how the shoulder moves. A scan rarely changes the treatment, so I wouldn’t spend your money on one.”
“Let’s think about the salon. Could your junior do the blow-drying for now? I can give you a fit note suggesting adapted duties if it helps with anything.”

f.learning: Frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) causes shoulder pain, often worse at night, followed by progressive stiffness with marked loss of both active and passive movement, typically affecting external rotation most. It is commonest between 40 and 60 and is more common in people with diabetes, so NICE CKS suggests checking for diabetes. It is a clinical diagnosis; imaging is not usually needed unless red flags or diagnostic doubt (an X-ray can exclude glenohumeral arthritis if movement is restricted after trauma or in older people). The condition usually passes through painful, stiff and recovery phases and most people improve, though it can take one to three years and some stiffness may remain. Management: analgesia, information, home exercises and physiotherapy, and an intra-articular corticosteroid injection, which can reduce pain and improve function in the early painful phase. In the UK FROST trial, early structured physiotherapy with a steroid injection was a reasonable first-line option, and surgical options offered no clear advantage for most people. Steroid injections can raise blood glucose for several days, which matters in diabetes. Refer if symptoms remain severe despite treatment. The consultation skill here is the hidden agenda: a refusal of blood tests before any are offered is a cue. Exploring it reveals fear rooted in a parent’s amputation; acknowledging that fear, explaining how different early diagnosis is, and linking the test to her own goals (a safe injection, keeping her business) makes it possible to agree an HbA1c. Supporting a self-employed patient’s work is part of good care.

Diagnose clinically, discuss injection, physiotherapy and analgesia honestly, explain why HbA1c matters for the shoulder and the injection, address the fear, and support her work.

points.t: Shoulder pain then stiffness with loss of active and passive movement, especially external rotation. Clinical diagnosis; imaging not routinely needed [1].
Trauma (fracture, dislocation), fever or hot joint (septic arthritis), weight loss or cancer history (metastasis, Pancoast tumour), neurological deficit, referred cardiac or neck pain.
Frozen shoulder is more common in diabetes; CKS suggests checking for it. Ask about thirst, nocturia, tiredness and previous results [1,3].
Painful phase, stiff phase and recovery phase over months to a few years. Most people improve; some stiffness may persist.

Analgesia, home exercises and physiotherapy. An intra-articular corticosteroid injection can help pain and function in the early phase. FROST: early physiotherapy plus injection is a reasonable first-line option; surgery offered no clear advantage for most [1,2].
Corticosteroid injections can raise blood glucose for several days; check HbA1c and advise people with diabetes to monitor (check the SPC) [5].
Consider referral if pain and stiffness remain severe despite treatment, or if the diagnosis is uncertain.
Discuss adaptations. A fit note can say “may be fit for work” with suggested adjustments, which can help self-employed people plan [4].

model.text: Hello Lorraine, I’m Dr Clarke. What can I help with today?
I need a steroid injection in this shoulder. My client had one and it was like magic. I can’t lift my arm to blow-dry and I’m losing clients. And before you ask, I don’t want any blood tests.
I can hear how much this is affecting your work. Let’s talk about the shoulder first, and I’ll come back to what you said about blood tests. When did it start?
model.why: Acknowledges; flags the cue to return to

model.text: About four months. Aching at first, now it’s agony at night and I can’t get my arm behind my back or do my bra up.
Did you injure it at all? Any fever, hot swollen joint, weight loss, cough, numbness or weakness in the arm, or chest pain when you’re active?
No, nothing like that.

Could you stand back from the camera? Lift both arms out to the side. Now keep your elbows tucked in and turn your hands outwards. Thank you. Your left shoulder is very restricted in all directions, especially turning outwards. That pattern fits a frozen shoulder. I’d like to check the passive movement face to face as well.
You said you don’t want blood tests before I’d mentioned any. Can I ask what makes you feel that way?
(pause) My mum had diabetes. She lost her leg. I know the last test was borderline. I’d rather not know.
That must have been really hard to see. It makes sense you’d want to avoid it. Have you noticed being thirsty, getting up at night to wee, or feeling more tired?
Thirsty all the time, and up twice a night. I put it down to my age.

Can I tell you why it matters for your shoulder? Frozen shoulder is more common when sugar levels run high. And a steroid injection can push sugar up for a few days, so I’d want to know your level to do the injection safely.
I didn’t know they were connected.

And if it is diabetes, finding it now is very different from your mum’s time. Today we look after feet, eyes and kidneys from the start, and many people get their sugars back down with changes and treatment.

Here’s what I suggest. A blood test for your sugar this week. If it’s safe, an injection into the shoulder joint, which can ease the pain at this stage, plus physiotherapy exercises, because the injection helps the pain but the exercises help the stiffness. Regular painkillers meanwhile.
Should I pay for an MRI?
I wouldn’t. The diagnosis comes from how your shoulder moves, and a scan rarely changes the treatment. Most frozen shoulders get better, but it can take a year or more, so we’ll keep reviewing it.
What about the salon? Could your junior take the blow-drying for a while? If it helps, I can write a fit note saying you may be fit for work with adapted duties.
She could do the drying. That would help.
So, what will you do this week?
Blood test. Then the injection and the physio. Junior does the drying. No MRI.

Perfect. If you get very thirsty, are weeing a lot, feel unwell or are losing weight, contact us sooner. And if the shoulder becomes hot and swollen, you get a fever, or arm weakness or numbness, get seen the same day.

social.t: No sick pay and fixed business costs make time off very hard. Work adaptations are often more useful than being signed off.
A parent’s complications can make people avoid diagnosis. Exploring this is often the key to engagement.

legal.t: Self-employed people can use a fit note. “May be fit for work” with suggested adaptations is often the most helpful option (DWP guidance).
She can decline a blood test. The doctor’s role is to inform, including the safety relevance to the injection, and to respect her decision.

professional.t: Declining an MRI that will not change management, with reasons, is responsible use of resources.
A refusal offered before a suggestion is a cue. Explore before persuading.

community.t: Many areas offer self-referral to MSK physiotherapy.
If the HbA1c is still in the non-diabetic hyperglycaemia range, offer referral to the programme.
